title: The birth of the newspaper
text: People have always traded news, but the newspaper as we know it required three things to come together: cheap paper, mechanical printing and widespread {{1}} (LITERATE). All three matured in northern Europe in the early seventeenth century, and within a few decades regular {{2}} (WEEK) were appearing in Strasbourg, Amsterdam and London. They were modest productions — a dozen pages of shipping news, commodity prices and reports of distant {{3}} (BATTLE) — but they established a habit that proved permanent. Censorship shaped their early {{4}} (DEVELOP), since rulers understood instinctively that controlling news meant controlling opinion. When England's licensing laws lapsed in 1695, a rough, {{5}} (ENERGY) and frequently libellous press erupted, and readers argued over the latest sheets in coffee houses, where the habit of {{6}} (ARGUE) about politics in public took firm root. By the nineteenth century, newspapers had become formidable businesses financed by {{7}} (ADVERTISE), and the proprietors who owned them discovered a strange new form of authority — the power to make a prime minister nervous before breakfast, an ability that struck contemporaries as dangerously {{8}} (POWER) for unelected men.

gaps.explanation: 'regular weeklies were appearing' — plural pinned by 'were'.
'reports of distant battles' — plural noun from battle.
'shaped their early development' — noun from develop.
'a rough, energetic press' — adjective from energy.
'the habit of arguing about politics' — gerund from argue.
